title: SBSQ #32: SuperMegaJumboDeluxe Edition
contentHtml:
The election is on Tuesday, and we’ll publish as much content as we can between now and then. But it’s also Halloween1, so let’s have a little fun today. This is the long-awaited (??) revival of Silver Bulletin Subscriber Questions (SBSQ). More specifically, it’s edition #32, which is obviously the Magic Johnson Edition. Most of the questions are election-related, but we’ll take a couple of sports ones at the end. But it’s also the SuperMegaJumboDeluxe Edition. We’re in lightning-round mode here; I’ll give you a couple of relatively off-the-cuff paragraphs on each topic.

You can leave questions for SBSQ #33 (the Larry Bird Edition) in the comments below. On the menu today:

  • Why is the Silver Bulletin mascot a wolf?

  • What’s up with the governors’ races in Alaska and Vermont?

  • What if Republicans win the House?

  • What if the polls froze?

  • Why didn’t 2018’s blue wave reach the Senate?

  • What should we make of big registered vs. likely voter gaps?

  • What can we learn from undecided voters?

  • Does FLIPR account for voter suppression or election interference?

  • The conservative golden age, revisited

  • Should models account for near-misses in sports?

  • Why isn’t there more baseball coverage at Silver Bulletin?

Why is the Silver Bulletin mascot a wolf?

Sophie asks:

Why is the Silver Bulletin mascot a wolf and not a dolphin (for FLIPR)?

Sylver, who is indeed a wolf 🐺, was recommended by Fivey Fox, and drawn by the same graphic artist as Fivey Fox. I think you’d agree that it would be pretty weird for a fox to be friends with a dolphin? Plus, FLIPR 🐬 can be a slippery fella. The reason we update the forecast only once per day is because we have to go find him in the East River — he’s never quite in the same location — and bribe him with sushi-grade tuna. Fivey, meanwhile, is living out his dreams by having become a ranger at Acadia National Park, where he never has to explain that 30 percent chances are supposed to happen 30 percent of the time.

What’s up with the governors’ races in Alaska and Vermont?

Jeremy asks:

The paid subscribers want to know what is happening with your gubernatorial forecast, specifically with Alaska and Vermont. Those are probably the forecasts where FLIPR is most going out on a limb. What are your feelings about those?

V. M. Kozma asks:

There is a large gap between FLIPR and prediction markets on the Alaska senate election that completely goes against the overall trend of prediction markets being less positive on Democrats’ chances.

An obvious explanation would be that the model fails to handle ranked choice voting.

Is there another explanation?

Also asked by Mike Shedlock, Trevor, Dan Rader and Kyle.

Yeah, these are two highly fascinating races. We covered the Alaska Senate race in last Sunday’s post. Since then, we’ve also added a scandal flag for Mary Peltola. (Because of her alleged abuse of campaign staffers; it’s more ambiguous whether the efforts to recruit other Dan Sullivans to the ballot would constitute a “scandal” by our standards.) It’s one major case where we’re lower on Democrats’ odds than the consensus.

But that’s also partly because of ranked-choice voting. It’s not because we’re failing to account for RCV; rather, I’d argue that it’s because we are handling RCV explicitly whereas other models are treating it as a rounding error:

Basically, the story would be that people are looking at the topline difference between Peltola and the “real” Dan Sullivan, where she’s ahead by a couple of points. But if Peltola doesn’t hit 50 percent in the first round and Sullivan picks up votes from the “fake” Dan Sullivan and the other Republican on the ballot, he could gain a point or so under ranked-choice voting reallocations

In the governor’s race, FLIPR has been very bullish on the Democrat, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, although we’re now aligned with the conventional wisdom there and it looks like Kreiss-Tomkins could win in the first round outright. That’s also because of RCV, although for a slightly different reason.

One mistake, as people might be making in Alaska’s Senate race, is to ignore RCV. But you can also err in the opposite direction by just summing up the cumulative vote for each party and assuming all votes transfer cleanly. In fact: (a) there is a fair bit of dropoff voting, i.e. voters don’t complete all options on their ballot; (b) maybe ~15 percent of voters switch parties with their second choices.

So if Kreiss-Tomkins is at 47 percent or something after the first round, it’s going to be very hard for any Republican opponent to catch up. Right now, we have the first round projected as follows:

  • Kreiss-Tomkins (D): 47.1 percent

  • Bernadette Wilson (R): 27.5 percent

  • Dave Bronson (R): 14.8 percent

  • Treg Taylor (R): 10.6 percent.

Nominally, the three Republicans have 52.9 percent of the projected first-round vote combined. But say 15 percent of Bronson and Taylor voters drop off, and another 15 percent flip to JKT. Then he winds up winning easily. On top of that, some polls ask about various runoff matchups, and we use that data directly where we can.

But look, this is tricky, and AK-Gov is certainly one of our more assumption-driven forecasts. Maybe 5-10 percent of the code in FLIPR is built for Alaska specifically. That doesn’t mean FLIPR is right. But it does mean we’re building in a whole host of logic about it, on top of the other assumptions that FLIPR employs.

Vermont, meanwhile, is one of the most difficult races to forecast on the map. Republican Phil Scott has repeatedly been re-elected by huge margins. But it’s a very, very blue state, obviously. According to “simple fundamentals”, which is just the generic ballot + Vermont’s partisan lean score, it should be roughly a D +40 state in a climate like this one. But “fancy fundamentals,” accounting for Scott’s big re-election margins, show an R +7 instead. Polls, meanwhile, have been all over the place, showing anything from a 15-point Scott lead to a 7-point lead for his opponent, Amanda Janoo. We land at about 70 percent for Scott being re-elected in FLIPR Deluxe, where he’s also helped by expert ratings being skeptical of the case for Janoo. We’ve mostly converged with prediction markets in Vermont, but it’s not the sort of race where I’d personally want to stake a lot of credibility. It’s a real throwback: more like the sort of races we’d get 20 or 30 years ago when candidate quality more often outweighed partisanship. Whereas our goal with FLIPR has mostly been to catch up with the trend of less and less crossover voting. The Senate race in Maine has some of these same characteristics. I think I’m comfortable with FLIPR’s heuristic of “yeah, Scott is probably the favorite, but who knows” because I can’t think of a better one, but VT-Gov will be one of the more high-impact races we look at internally for evaluating FLIPR, even if it isn’t getting much attention from the national media.

Paid subscribers get full access to our Election Night livestream and live blog with updates from our friends at The Argument, GD Politics and Slow Boring.

What if Republicans win the House?

Alex asks:

You wake up tomorrow and it’s the morning of November 4th. Although there are still some California races to be called, it looks like Republicans hit the inside straight on election night and will retain both the House and Senate. What happened? What did the polls completely miss?

So, I’m not going to 100 percent promise this — these plans might get upended if there are crazy swings in the polls over the weekend. But if things are relatively calm, I’m planning on running through a bunch of “morning after” scenarios. What do the relatively normal outcomes look like on the map, according to FLIPR, and then what about the weird ones?

Republicans winning the House would be weird: a 95th+ percentile outcome for the party, not an 80th percentile one. And just to be clear, if Republicans have won the House, that’s almost certainly a major disaster for Democrats in the Senate.
